body:
in Art, History |   	September 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

With the Bayeux Tapes­try now on dis­play at the British Muse­um, Deep Down His­to­ry presents a deep dive into the embroi­dery’s full sto­ry:
“The Bayeux Tapes­try is one of the most remark­able sur­vivals of the Mid­dle Ages — a 70 metre embroi­dered account of the events lead­ing to the Nor­man Con­quest of Eng­land in 1066, cul­mi­nat­ing in the Bat­tle of Hast­ings. This video tells the Tapes­try’s sto­ry in full, using Charles Stothard’s ear­ly colour repro­duc­tion, pre­sent­ed here as a seam­less scroll for the first time. We fol­low Harold God­win­son’s fate­ful jour­ney from Edward the Con­fes­sor’s court to Nor­mandy, his lat­er seizure of the Crown, and William the Con­queror’s inva­sion. Beyond its polit­i­cal mes­sag­ing, the Tapes­try is also burst­ing with medieval his­to­ry, includ­ing jokes, fas­ci­nat­ing tech­ni­cal details, and a warn­ing for those who break their promis­es…”
Enjoy!
via Kot­tke

title: Rage Against the Machines: From the Luddites to the AI Data Center Backlash
description:
in History, Technology |   	September 18th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One often-repeat­ed anec­dote about Mil­ton Fried­man has the famous eco
body:
in History, Technology |   	September 18th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One often-repeat­ed anec­dote about Mil­ton Fried­man has the famous econ­o­mist vis­it­ing a canal under con­struc­tion in nine­teen-six­ties Chi­na. Notic­ing the sheer num­ber of human labor­ers dig­ging away with shov­els, he asked the offi­cial in charge why they weren’t get­ting the work done faster with exca­va­tors and oth­er mod­ern machines. The bureau­crat explained to him that doing it by hand cre­at­ed more jobs. Fried­man’s reply: “If it’s jobs you want, you should give those men spoons instead.” Whether or not this exchange ever actu­al­ly hap­pened, it illus­trates a con­flict that’s arisen more than once in the his­to­ry of civ­i­liza­tion, pos­si­bly since the dawn of indus­tri­al­iza­tion — and at least since the hey­day of the Lud­dites.
Accord­ing to the Uni­ver­si­ty of Cam­bridge, that hey­day came in 1812, the year of “an assault by some 150 armed labor­ers on a Hud­der­s­field mill, in which sol­diers opened fire on the mob to stop them break­ing into the premis­es, fatal­ly wound­ing two attack­ers.” This was the cul­mi­na­tion of a series of protests across Eng­land, all of them inspired by anger at “new tech­nolo­gies, like auto­mat­ed looms, which were being used in the tex­tile indus­try in place of the skilled work of arti­sans, threat­en­ing their liveli­hoods as a result.” These des­per­ate­ly infu­ri­at­ed pro­test­ers, whose doc­u­ment­ed actions include the mur­der of a York­shire mill own­er, loud­ly expressed alle­giance to one Ned Ludd, a weaver said to have tak­en the bold step of smash­ing a cou­ple of new­fan­gled stock­ing frames some 25 years before.
The sto­ry of Lud­d’s ear­ly stand against mech­a­niza­tion may be even more ques­tion­able than the one about Mil­ton Fried­man and the spoons, but his name sur­vives today nev­er­the­less. In fact, it’s under­gone some­what of a revival thanks to the arti­fi­cial-intel­li­gence boom of recent years, dur­ing which even the mod­ern “knowl­edge work­ers” have come to fear the tram­pling of their liveli­hoods under tech­nol­o­gy’s inex­orable march. Their calls for restric­tions on the devel­op­ment and deploy­ment of AI are, in one side’s fram­ing of the argu­ment, mere­ly the lat­est pub­lic spasm of Lud­dism, a move­ment explained in the video above from The His­to­ry Guy. How many here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, after all, would argue that the mass pro­duc­tion of socks ulti­mate­ly con­sti­tut­ed a real loss for human­i­ty?
Lud­dism nev­er did count a large pro­por­tion of the Eng­lish labor force as its own. Rather, the move­ment appealed to “a rel­a­tive­ly ‘elite’ group” of legal­ly pro­tect­ed work­ers only allowed into their pro­fes­sions after years of appren­tice­ship, at which point “they tend­ed to feel that they were owed a liv­ing.” Nor did the con­di­tions, hours, and com­pen­sa­tion at the fac­to­ries then spring­ing up seem favor­able com­pared to the way of life enjoyed by their pre­de­ces­sors. Sim­i­lar sen­ti­ments may under­lie the “Lud­dite clubs” form­ing on col­lege cam­pus­es, on which NPR has report­ed, or this year’s social media-free “Sum­mer of Ludd” at the New School, to say noth­ing of ongo­ing protests against data-cen­ter con­struc­tion. It would be fas­ci­nat­ing to hear what gen­uine nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry Lud­dites would make of our sit­u­a­tion. Per­haps, one day, we can use AI to res­ur­rect them.

title: How Reading Changes the Way Your Brain Works
description:
in Books, Psychology |   	September 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Read­ing is unnat­ur­al. This will hard­ly come as a sur­prise to any chil
body:
in Books, Psychology |   	September 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Read­ing is unnat­ur­al. This will hard­ly come as a sur­prise to any child try­ing to put off his home­work for just one more hour of watch­ing oth­er kids play Minecraft. Yet there real­ly are impli­ca­tions worth con­sid­er­ing if we accept that our cog­ni­tive sys­tems did­n’t evolve to process text in the same way as they evolved to han­dle vision and speech. Speak­ing on an evo­lu­tion­ary his­tor­i­cal scale, “we haven’t had enough time to devel­op a ded­i­cat­ed read­ing brain,” says UCLA neu­ro­sci­en­tist Rebec­ca Gotlieb in the BBC World Ser­vice video above. For the time being, in a kind of cog­ni­tive jer­ry-rig­ging, “we co-opt parts of the brain involved in vision and audi­to­ry pro­cess­ing and lan­guage and atten­tion and affect.”
That was true for read­ers and writ­ers of Sumer­ian cuneiform and Egypt­ian hiero­glyph­ics five mil­len­nia ago. It still is for read­ers and writ­ers of the many scripts in use today, from the Latin alpha­bet to Chi­nese char­ac­ters to the Ara­bic abjad, each of which has its own influ­ence on its users’ neu­ro­log­i­cal archi­tec­ture. One of the biggest dif­fer­ences between then and now is the scale of read­ing: ancient Sume­ria and Egypt seem to have had lit­er­a­cy rates around one per­cent, a num­ber com­pris­ing most­ly scribes, priests, and nobles, while the glob­al aver­age today comes in around 88 per­cent and ris­ing. Anoth­er is the medi­um of read­ing: the shift from papyrus to paper may have seemed remark­able at the time, but the more recent one from paper to elec­tron­ic screens has already changed the way we think about our world.
“When we read on screens, we tend to skim, and when we skim, we’re more sus­cep­ti­ble to mis­in­for­ma­tion,” says Gotlieb. So we’ve been told, many times and many ways, amid the past decade’s ever-more-trou­bled polit­i­cal reportage. In 2018, Maryanne Wolf, author of Come Home: The Read­ing Brain in a Dig­i­tal World, argued in the Guardian that the “sub­tle atro­phy of crit­i­cal analy­sis and empa­thy” appar­ent­ly caused by tech­nol­o­gy-encour­aged skim­ming “affects our abil­i­ty to nav­i­gate a con­stant bom­bard­ment of infor­ma­tion. It incen­tivizes a retreat to the most famil­iar silos of unchecked infor­ma­tion, which require and receive no analy­sis, leav­ing us sus­cep­ti­ble to false infor­ma­tion and dem­a­goguery.”
So much for us adults. What about the chil­dren? In the BBC World Ser­vice video, Wolf blunt­ly sums up the results of stud­ies so far on the effects of ear­ly read­ing expe­ri­ence on lat­er intel­lec­tu­al per­for­mance: “the more dig­i­tal, the worse aca­d­e­m­ic.” If a young brain is “con­stant­ly being dis­tract­ed and hyper­stim­u­lat­ed, you’re going to have them not able to real­ly move from one stim­u­lus to the next with­out a desire for ever-quick­er inter­vals between stim­uli.” For our part, as par­ents, teach­ers, or oth­er vis­i­ble exam­ples of grown-uphood, we can do noth­ing to coun­ter­act that more effec­tive­ly than to mod­el and enjoy a rich “read­ing life” for the next gen­er­a­tion. We must, in oth­er words, pick up books and not put them down, which may strike an Open Cul­ture read­er as an easy task. But ask your­self this: how many times did you click over to some­thing else before get­ting to the end of this post?

title: Across Two Exhibitions, Jaume Plensa's Monumental Sculptures Unite Scale and Material
description: Measuring 28 feet wide and seven feet tall, two monumental wooden relief sculptures anchor Beyond Silence, a new exhibition at GRAY Chicago featur
body:
Measuring 28 feet wide and seven feet tall, two monumental wooden relief sculptures anchor Beyond Silence, a new exhibition at GRAY Chicago featuring works by Catalan artist and sculptor Jaume Plensa.
The broad works—titled “Julia” and “Maria”—were created as part of the artist’s recent series, Beyond Silence, which shares a name with the show. The two paneled pieces transform the gallery’s open exhibition space with their rigid angles, creating a structured rhythm to complement the subdued contours of the faces they depict. As a result, a conversation arises between Plensa’s signature overarching motifs, such as the human figure, use of architectural materials, and the perception of space.
“Maria” (2026). Cast iron and granite stone, 85 3⁄8 × 62 7⁄8 × 109 3⁄8 inches
Surrounding these wooden reliefs, viewers encounter dramatically elongated faces stretching seven feet high. The impressive portraits are part of Plensa’s Clouds series, in which the artist pairs cast iron—a material often associated with commercialism and industry—with the suavity of granite stone, “producing an unexpected sense of suspension and weightlessness,” the gallery says. 
Like many of Plensa’s works, the large faces stand with their eyes closed, allowing viewers to experience each monumental figure intimately. These impressive pieces evoke a quiet stillness and offer a unique space for introspection, meditation, and a sense of intimacy through shared humanity. 
Beyond Silence marks the artist’s tenth solo exhibition with GRAY, and coincides with Remote, Serene, Ethereal opening next week at the gallery’s New York location. Both exhibitions are on view through December 19. And if you’re in Chicago, you can always find Plensa’s iconic work, Crown Fountain, at Millennium Park. Find more from the artist on Instagram.

title: South Tyrol's Bunkers Shoulder WWII History in Vincenzo Pagliuca's Portraits
description: Italy’s South Tyrol province, which borders Switzerland and Austria in the Alps and is home to some of Central Europe’s most dramatic mountains, l
body:
Italy’s South Tyrol province, which borders Switzerland and Austria in the Alps and is home to some of Central Europe’s most dramatic mountains, lives up to its geographic position as a borderland. Italy annexed the region in 1919 following World War I, prior to which it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Many people are German-speaking, and in many ways, their cultural traditions and ancestry lean traditionally toward Austria more than Italy.
At the outbreak of World War II, the Fascist Italian regime built a series of fortifications along the country’s northernmost border. Construction was halted at the onset of the war, and the military controlled what had been completed until 1993. For Vincenzo Pagliuca, these purpose-built structures spurred an intrepid yet pensive body of work called Bunker, published in hardcover by Hartmann Books.
“Opera 1 Anterselva”
Many of the bunkers are freestanding concrete masses with distinctive domed shapes and thick walls. Others take advantage of the ancient pre-existing stone, sometimes carving directly into mountainsides and augmenting with extra barriers. Over the years, grasses have colonized the roofs, shrubs have grown close, and some of the exteriors, which were designed to camouflage against the slopes like exposed rock, have a surreal, almost Gaudí-esque character.
Pagliuca has long been fascinated by Italian architecture, such as in his project Mónos, which highlights the often quirky vernacular of diminutive homes. For Bunker, he was interested in the relationship of these specific structures to their rarefied and remote locations, their solidity and often hulking presence at odds with the surrounding Alpine meadows and soaring, snow-capped peaks.
These human interventions, depicted without the presence of people, are a permanent reminder of the drastic measures that political and military forces will go in the name of nationalism. “The bunkers represent a difficult legacy, recalling a dramatic historical period in Central Europe marked by nationalist ideology and the inability to resolve conflicts through peaceful means—an era we thought had long since passed,” says a statement from the publisher. 
Grab a copy of your own from the publisher’s shop. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Step Inside the Studios of 20 Contemporary Black Artists in 'Another View'
description: One of the most intimate windows into an artist’s practice is their studio. While some creatives thrive on methodical organization and tidiness, o
body:
One of the most intimate windows into an artist’s practice is their studio. While some creatives thrive on methodical organization and tidiness, others reach their flow state amid a cluttered chaos where dozens of ideas unfold at once. Whether at one end of this spectrum or somewhere in the middle, these spaces offer unique perspectives on both the artist and the masterpieces that emerge from their confines.
Forthcoming from Phaidon, Another View: The Vibrant World of Contemporary Black Artists invites readers into 20 distinctive studios. Celebrating some of the most prominent artists working today—such as Nick Cave, Nina Chanel Abney, Hank Willis Thomas, Carrie Mae Weems, Kerry James Marshall, and many more—the seminal volume highlights a range of behind-the-scenes material.
Hank Willis Thomas, Brooklyn 
The introduction to Another View was written by lauded literary critic, filmmaker, and professor Henry Louis Gates, Jr. who “explores the historical precedents and critical context that led to the exciting current moment of Black contemporary art in America,” writes Phaidon. Across nearly 200 pages, the book includes 150 never-before-seen photographs, exclusive interviews, and profiles.
Another View: The Vibrant World of Contemporary Black Artists is slated for release on October 28. Pre-order your copy in the Colossal Shop.

title: Through Carved Wooden Assemblages, Daniel Minter Communes with the Spiritual
description: Walk into the first gallery of the group exhibition Thresholds at the Haggerty Museum of Art, and you’ll encounter dozens of hand brooms installed
body:
Walk into the first gallery of the group exhibition Thresholds at the Haggerty Museum of Art, and you’ll encounter dozens of hand brooms installed in long rows. Scraps of ribbons, cords, and braids in a vast array of colors and textures bind the small tools together, with raw branches from a fallen tree jutting from the top. Made during a participatory workshop this past July  at Lynden Sculpture Garden, the sweepers are what artist Daniel Minter calls a “talisman, tool, and object of remembrance.”
Minter has long considered the spiritual dimension of the items we use in daily life. The broom, for example, has been an ongoing topic of inquiry as he questions what it means to cleanse and care for one’s space and self and how those acts of devotion are also ones that bring empowerment. It’s fitting that Minter sees his work as a service, a sort of public offering he can provide through sculpture, drawing, community projects, and more.

Based in Portland, Maine, for more than two decades, Minter was raised in Georgia during Jim Crow. He and his family lived across the street from a white-only swimming pool, and schools were segregated until the artist reached fourth grade. “When you start seeing the systems that create these inequalities, you also can begin to notice systems that empower you,” he says one morning over a video call. “You notice the systems that give you a stronger sense of yourself.”
One of the latter was his mother’s near constant singing and the artist’s own desire to create. As an adolescent, Minter would carve small sticks and paint signs for neighbors who needed them. He went on to study in illustration in college and today, still collaborates on the occasional children’s book. His work for Going Down Home with Daddy even won the prestigious Caldecott Medal.
At the Haggerty Museum, we witness Minter’s multi-faceted practice. In addition to the community-created display of brooms, the artist presents vibrant carved sculptures painted with stylized portraits and superimposed motifs. The figurative assemblages combine found objects with carefully selected materials that, as the artist sees it, become vessels for spiritual and ancestral knowledge. 
“I came from a people with a long and complex tradition of creating exactly these kinds of tools—objects of communication and transformation,” Minter writes in a catalog essay for Thresholds, which pairs the museum’s holdings with the artist’s sculptures. “The objects and masks from the Haggerty Museum collection bring my work into direct contact with that timeless technology. They allow me to see my carving as a way of reconnecting with and continuinga living system of communication with the spirits, the ancestors, the unseen.”

Minter is also intentional about setting the scene for such communion to occur. Nature is the foundation, and each wall within his part of the exhibition represents a different facet: blue for the ocean, red for fire and thunder, and green for the forest. Verdant settings also appear in the central, freestanding sculpture, which positions an abstract, totemic figure atop astroturf. 
Typically presented outdoors or in a forest, the two-sided form is Minter’s way of instilling hope. “How do you find the things you need to see a future when the objects before you say different?” he asks. This sculpture is the artist’s answer to that question and way of offering peace to anyone who encounters the piece and is willing to listen to its message.
“Do objects transmit spirituality? No, they remind us of our spirituality. They allow us to translate. A particular object can remind you that you can think deeply and pass this obstacle that is in front of you,” he adds. “That’s a service.” 
Thresholds is on view through December 19 at the Haggerty, which is part of Milwaukee’s Marquette University. Explore Minter’s practice on his website and Instagram.
